Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has recently become widowed, has been working as a nanny in a suburban household since retiring from his previous job in retail. His life took an unexpected and harrowing turn when he witnessed the life-threatening illness of one of the children he was caring for—a young girl named Lily. The trauma began late one evening when Lily suddenly started convulsing and losing consciousness. Mr. Tran immediately called for emergency services, but during that time, he found himself frozen in fear and unable to act effectively. The ambulance eventually arrived, and Lily was rushed to the hospital where she spent several days in critical condition before slowly stabilizing. Since then, Mr. Tran has been struggling with a host of symptoms that have significantly impacted his daily life. He avoids seeking medical care for himself, despite experiencing occasional chest pains and other concerning health issues. Each time he considers visiting a doctor, memories of Lily’s convulsions flood back, leaving him feeling overwhelmed and frightened. This avoidance extends to psychological help as well; the thought of discussing his experiences is unbearable. Mr. Tran has also adopted a strategy of suppressing thoughts about the traumatic event. He tries hard not to think about what happened, often telling himself that he needs to focus on other things to keep his mind occupied. However, this constant mental distraction takes its toll. Mr. Tran finds himself frequently distracted at work, which has led to several minor mishaps and moments of forgetfulness, causing him some anxiety about maintaining the trust of the family he works for. Despite these efforts, his memories of Lily’s illness remain vivid and feel more real than ordinary events in his life. He often relives those moments, feeling as though they are happening right now rather than something that is over. The memory of her convulsions triggers intense emotional responses whenever he sees anything similar—like a child having a minor seizure or even just falling down. Mr. Tran’s sense of self has been deeply affected by this event. He feels unrecognizable to himself, believing that the person who once cared for children with joy and confidence is now someone who lives in constant fear and anxiety. This shift has made him distrustful of others, as he sees them not as supportive but as potentially dangerous or deceptive. His core belief is that he has permanently changed for the worse, and this conviction weighs heavily on his daily life. The combination of these symptoms and his increasing isolation have taken a toll on Mr. Tran’s relationships with the family he works for. He avoids discussing any concerns about Lily’s health out of fear it will trigger another episode, but this avoidance has led to misunderstandings and tension within the household. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was an incident where he became so overwhelmed by memories during a walk that he felt dizzy and disoriented. He realized that his constant attempts to avoid and suppress these experiences were no longer sustainable and that he needed professional support to navigate this challenging time in his life. Mr. Tran is most afraid of losing control over his own mind and emotions, feeling as though the trauma has fundamentally altered who he is. However, he also hopes for a way to regain some sense of normalcy and trust in himself and others. He wants to find a path forward that allows him to continue caring for children without being overwhelmed by the memories of Lily’s illness.
